about: Every claim the page shows, with the mark the source gives it. Status: verified (the note or addendum read it in code, a spec or a paper section; 'computed' arithmetic of Addendum D is verified here too, and scripts/check.py reproduces it) | unverified (the source says so, or the note gives no mark) | inferred (the source tags it as inference) | ours (a design choice of this thesis). 'n' = the row in the claims-vs-evidence table of the note named in 'loc' (the hop-depth note, or the graph-algorithms note for src note2 and locators that say 'algorithms note'), when there is one. The graph-algorithms note's [decided] label maps to 'ours'.

claims.text: The walk is a breadth-first search with a relation mask, depth at most 2; each concept keeps its shortest hop.
Rule 7 puts all 10 graph slots at hop 0: 120 of 120 graph-list items in 6 stored hybrid turns, and 10 of 10 demo questions.
One seed concept has 38-456 passages. One demo question reached 38 passages at hop 0, 174 at hop 1, 287 at hop 2 and 547 at hop 3.
An adaptive depth would not fix the hop-0 problem: the cut happens after the walk.
Hop-balanced gives 4/3/3 at depth 2 with 10 slots (7/7/6 with 20, 10/10/10 with 30) when every hop holds at least its quota.
Codex's test cases with 10 slots: hop sizes {500, 1, 1} give 8/1/1 with backfill and 4/1/1 (6 passages) without; {500, 300, 1} give 6/3/1 with backfill and 4/3/1 (8 passages) without.
With backfill the rule fills min(want, N) slots, and the deeper passages chosen by the quota pass stay. No relevance benefit is claimed: the reason is capacity only.
The chosen passages keep hop-first order in the list, so fusion and packing can still push deeper passages out of the context.
Pilot 1 as run (placeholder router, k_graph 20): 29 of 30 graph lists were all hop 0; one item had 3 hop-0 and 17 hop-1 passages.

Under the earlier frozen configuration with rule 7, H and Hc retrieval would be identical on 30 of 30 pilot items. This projection assumes pilot 2 links the same seeds as pilot 1, and that assumption is not verified.

Balanced ranking needs cross-encoder scores for every passage at hops 0-2. Pilot 30 items: 118,691 pairs (hop 0: 7,529; hop 1: 35,059; hop 2: 76,103); 107,871 were new when Addendum D was written. All were scored and merged before tuning (see the scoring-sources lesson).
About 181.6k new pairs at about 0.5 pairs per second is about 100 kernel-hours on Kaggle CPU. This is an extrapolation, not a demonstration; the scoring-sources lesson gives the measured rate.
Under router s7-b/2, 15 of 30 pilot questions take the fallback row (all relations, both directions), where H = Hc.
Thesis: keep a fixed, pre-registered depth of 2 and the fixed quota rule hop-balanced/1. One rule, fixed before data; no grid over quota formulas.
Product: next try a PPR or hop-decay score (no LLM calls). That it would beat the quota is a proposal; no test exists yet.
A hop-decay score (CE x gamma^hop, one global gamma) is soft like PathRAG's alpha, with one parameter to tune.
2-3 concept hops are enough for course questions. No study exists; only our 10 demo chains, which reach their targets at hop 2 or 3.
The 10 demo chains of our KG reach their targets at hop 2 or 3 (for example kernel trick, Mercer kernel, positive definite matrix, eigenvalue).
Packing order matters: models use the start and the end of the context best. Abstract read only, not the method.
GraphRAG global search does not walk. It picks a community level and ranks community answers by an LLM helpfulness score (0-100), added until the token limit.

GraphRAG local search takes seed entities plus their one-hop relations and splits the context by fixed token proportions (text units 0.5, community reports 0.15; context 12k tokens). Defaults may change by version.
LightRAG adds the one-hop neighbours of the matched entities and relations.
HippoRAG has no depth: Personalized PageRank from the query nodes (damping 0.5) scores passages. Single-step retrieval is about as good as iterative IRCoT, 10-20x cheaper and 6-13x faster.
HippoRAG 2 seeds PPR with phrase nodes and all passage nodes (weight 0.05 tested).
Think-on-Graph: an LLM-guided beam search stops when the LLM judges the paths sufficient or at D_max; width = depth = 3; at most 2ND+D+1 LLM calls (25 at N = D = 3); gains flatten past depth 3.
Think-on-Graph 2.0 scores an entity by an exponentially decayed sum of its top chunk scores; a BGE reranker was best for pruning; plateau past depth 3.
Reasoning on Graphs: an LLM plans relation paths (top 3), then a constrained BFS follows them.
G-Retriever has no depth: a prize-collecting Steiner tree, where an edge cost controls the subgraph size.
GRAG uses fixed 2-hop ego-graphs: 2-hop beats 1-hop; past 3 hops the embeddings oversmooth.

PathRAG has no hop limit: flow decays by alpha = 0.7 per edge and weak paths are cut. Its flow order beat a hop-first order (55.64% win rate, LLM judge on summary-style questions: weak evidence for our task).
GNN-RAG: WebQSP questions need up to 2 hops, CWQ up to 4.
IRCoT: one reasoning sentence, one retrieval; it stops at "answer is" or a step limit; at most 15 paragraphs.
Adaptive-RAG: a small classifier picks no retrieval, single-step or multi-step before retrieval.
Self-RAG retrieves when its Retrieve token passes a threshold (0.2 for most tasks).
FLARE retrieves when the next sentence has low-probability tokens; DRAGIN uses an entropy-attention score.
KG-GPT, StructGPT, KAG and Self-Ask let an LLM split the question or call tools until it can answer. The note lists them without a verification mark.
Multi-hop benchmark questions need 2-4 hops: MuSiQue has 2-4-hop questions; HotpotQA is built from two paragraphs per question.
A survey frame: once, iterative (fixed or adaptive) and multi-stage retrieval; ranking and pruning cut what was retrieved. Our pipeline is once retrieval, non-adaptive, then cross-encoder pruning.

H and H-collapsed run the same walk code; they differ only in one argument of the walk, eligible(edge, route). In H the relation mask filters edges; in H-collapsed every concept-to-concept edge is allowed.

The walk is a BFS because the thesis tests typed edges: with a mask, a masked edge is never followed, so any difference between H and H-collapsed comes from the labels. PPR or communities would add a second moving part.

The primary items are in the prerequisite or cross-concept strata of one course and need 1-3 concept hops from named concepts; they are not 'summarise the course' questions. The strata are decided; the link to BFS is inferred.
Walk&Retrieve: a BFS corpus beats random walks on MetaQA (Hits@1 67.99 vs 55.60).
HippoRAG ablation: average R@5 72.9 with PPR, 59.2 with the seeds plus their 1-hop neighbours, 56.2 with the seeds only. The neighbour variant is not a BFS + rerank pipeline like ours.
HippoRAG is lower than ColBERTv2 on HotpotQA (R@5 77.7 vs 79.3).
HippoRAG 2 average F1 59.8 vs the dense retriever NV-Embed-v2 57.0, GraphRAG 49.6 and LightRAG 6.6 (the LightRAG figure is the authors' reproduction).
Index input tokens on 11,656 passages: GraphRAG 115.5M, LightRAG 68.5M, HippoRAG 2 9.2M.

LEGO-GraphRAG: PPR beats random walks; it is preferred over k-hop for control of the subgraph size, not for a measured quality gap. PPR takes 0.58 s at 100K nodes and 75 s at 100M nodes. Entity-answer KGQA, so the transfer to text passages is inferred.

Xiang's GraphRAG-Bench: vanilla RAG is as good as or better than GraphRAG on fact retrieval; HippoRAG 2 (PPR) has the best cost-quality at about 1k prompt tokens; Microsoft GraphRAG global search uses about 331k prompt tokens per query (figure; the paper's text gives a different value).
GraphRAG global search: 72-83 % comprehensiveness win rate vs vector RAG on global questions (LLM judge); a graph-free map-reduce gets most of this gain.
Community-global search answers Null queries with 19.27 % accuracy vs 96.01 % for plain RAG.
A token-matched RAG ties community-local search (69.33 vs 69.01).

claims.text: LLM-judge verdicts flip when the answer order is swapped.
DIGIMON (19 operators, one framework, top-k 4 for every method): methods that return source chunks win specific QA; community-global search costs 353,889 tokens per query vs 1,680 for vanilla RAG.
The thesis plans PPR as a later retrieval stage or an exploratory baseline; it is not part of the primary comparison.
Plain PPR treats every edge the same. A label-aware version needs a weight per relation type, a new parameter to tune; H vs H-collapsed would then test labels plus tuned weights.
PPR has no depth: every reachable concept gets a score, so it changes the candidate set and the ranking together, and the comparison with the frozen depth-2 rule would no longer be like for like.
Community summaries are built for global sensemaking questions over corpora of about 1M tokens; our items ask about one concept and its prerequisites.
A community summary hides which edge type joined its members, so the thesis could not test the labels through it.
No recorded decision on community detection for retrieval; in the product, Louvain only colours the graph in the UI.
No benchmark compares PPR, Leiden communities and k-hop BFS on one text-built graph with one token budget (abstract-level search).
Product: for overview questions, retrieve pre-written summaries per lecture or per community by vector search, not full map-reduce. A proposal; lecture summaries as a first version are an inference.
